value.overview: The Yellow-bellied Sapsucker is a medium-sized, migratory woodpecker of North and Central America. It is named for its habit of drilling orderly rows of holes, or sapwells, in living trees and feeding on the sap and insects they attract. Bold black-and-white barring, a red forehead, and yellowish underparts help identify it. Males also have a red throat. The species breeds in northern forests and spends the nonbreeding season farther south, including Costa Rica.
value.classification: The Yellow-bellied Sapsucker belongs to the woodpecker family Picidae and the genus Sphyrapicus. Its scientific name is Sphyrapicus varius.
value.identification: This sapsucker measures about 34–40 cm in wingspan and has a strongly patterned black-and-white face and body. Adults show a red forehead, a broad white wing stripe, and pale yellow or whitish underparts. Males have a conspicuous red throat, while females usually have a pale throat. Juveniles are duller and lack the strong adult red markings. Its upright posture on tree trunks, slightly stiff tail support, and neatly aligned sapwells are useful field clues. The drumming is irregular and stuttering.
value.rangeHabitat: The Yellow-bellied Sapsucker breeds across much of Canada, the northeastern and north-central United States, and parts of the Appalachian region. During the nonbreeding season it moves through the southern United States, Mexico, Central America, and locally the Caribbean, reaching Panama. In Costa Rica it occurs as a wintering migrant and passage migrant rather than a regular breeding species. It uses wooded habitats ranging from lowland and foothill forests to montane areas, including forest edges, open woodland, gardens, plantations, and second-growth vegetation with suitable trees.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Most individuals leave the breeding range in autumn and winter in the southern United States, Mexico, and Central America. In Costa Rica, it is principally present from roughly October or November through March or April, with some records during migration outside the main winter period; it is not known as a regular breeder there.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place mainly from late spring through summer in deciduous and mixed forests. Pairs excavate a nest cavity, usually in a living tree with softened or decayed wood, often an aspen, birch, maple, beech, or elm. The male commonly performs most of the excavation. The cavity is lined only with wood chips. A typical clutch contains several white eggs, and both parents participate in incubation and care of the young. Nest cavities may be reused in later years.
value.dietFeeding: Sap is a major food, obtained by drilling two general types of sapwells into tree bark. The bird regularly maintains these holes so sap continues to flow, then laps it with a brush-tipped tongue. It also eats ants and other insects, spiders, cambium, and occasionally fruit. Insects may be gleaned from bark or captured in short aerial sallies. In Costa Rica, it can forage in wooded habitats where suitable living trees provide sap and insect prey.
value.behavior: Yellow-bellied Sapsuckers often cling quietly to trunks while inspecting or feeding at sapwells. They defend feeding areas and breeding territories with vocal calls, displays, and distinctive irregular drumming on resonant wood or metal. Sapwells can attract hummingbirds and other animals, creating temporary feeding opportunities for several species. Individuals are generally solitary outside the breeding season, although several birds may use productive trees or overlapping woodland habitats during migration and winter.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered stable to increasing, although trends can vary among regions and monitoring programs.
